title: Heart rate, body size and lifespan in mammals (Garger et al. 2023 supplementary data; Zhang & Zhang 2009; Levine 1997)

sources.publisher: Aging Cell (via PubMed Central, U.S. National Library of Medicine)
sources.title: Garger D. et al. (2023) The impact of the cardiovascular component and somatic mutations on ageing. Aging Cell 22(10): e13957
sources.note: 動物數值取自 Supplementary Table 1（1a Lifespan、1c Resting heart rate、1e Adult mass；附件 ACEL-22-e13957-s002.xlsx，經 Europe PMC 的補充檔下載）。lifespan＝人類照顧下 80% 個體死亡時的年齡（Cagan et al. 2022）；adult mass 取自 AnAge

facts.text: Mouse: adult mass 20.5 g, resting heart rate about 664 beats per minute (663.88), lifespan 3.7 years (3.68).
Naked mole-rat: adult mass 35 g, resting heart rate about 227 beats per minute (227.39), lifespan 25.3 years (25.35).
Rat: adult mass 300 g, resting heart rate about 345 beats per minute (345.2), lifespan 2.7 years (2.75).
Rabbit: adult mass 1,800 g (1.8 kg), resting heart rate about 240 beats per minute (240.01), lifespan 9.1 years (9.13).
Dog: adult mass 40,000 g (40 kg), resting heart rate about 103 beats per minute (103.26), lifespan 15.3 years (15.26).
Human: adult mass 62,035 g (about 62 kg), resting heart rate 73 beats per minute (adults aged 20 to 39), lifespan 83.7 years (83.67).
Lion: adult mass 175,000 g (175 kg), resting heart rate 59.5 beats per minute (about 60), lifespan 20.6 years (20.64).
Horse: adult mass 300,000 g (300 kg), resting heart rate about 40 beats per minute (40.15), lifespan 31.5 years (31.53).
In this 2023 dataset, lifespan means the age by which 80 percent of animals kept by people had died; adult mass comes from the AnAge database.
Resting heart rate in mammals runs from about 30 to 35 beats per minute in whales and elephants up to 600 to 700 in mice.
Very small mammals such as mice and rats have the fastest hearts and shortest lives; large mammals such as elephants and whales have the slowest hearts and longest lives.
A faster resting heart rate goes with a faster basal metabolic rate.
Small mammals have more body surface for their weight, so they need a higher metabolic rate to keep their body temperature steady.
For each kilogram of body weight, small animals use oxygen much faster than large ones.
Multiplying heart rate by life span gives a lifetime total that stays roughly the same across most warm-blooded mammals, around one billion (1 x 10^9) beats.
Judging by heart rate alone, humans would be expected to live about as long as tigers and giraffes (roughly 20 years), yet human hearts make about three billion beats in a lifetime.
For most of human history the average life span was under 30 years; today’s long lives owe much to medical knowledge and to disease control and prevention.
The naked mole-rat lives about five times longer than expected for its body mass.
Levine (1997) concluded that heart rate is a marker of metabolic rate and that the link between heart rate and life span is a side effect rather than a direct cause.
In a mouse study (Gent et al.), the drug ivabradine lowered heart rate by 14 percent and raised median lifespan by 6.2 percent.
The 2023 study (Garger et al.) gathered these values for 15 mammal species to study ageing.

notes: 表格用 s1 Supplementary Table 1 的 8 種動物（依體重排序），數字四捨五入：心跳取整數、壽命取一位小數、體重 g／kg 依大小換算。
